Why a Linux-powered botnet shouldn't send you scurrying back to Windows

TL:DR

Dumbass server admins that can't do the most basic of security, such as: Disable root account login, disable text login, only use SSH keyfiles, change default port/port knocking, use fail2ban or the likes.

Its not even maleware, its just someone automating the guessing of peoples passwords.

Ubuntu isn't the only major Linux distro that's not vulnerable to this malware out of the box. The default release of Linux Mint, another very popular distribution, doesn't include the remote access software the malware needs to break into the machine.

It also isn't right to say this malware is exploiting a bug at the heart of the Linux OS, instead it takes over machines by brute forcing access to the root user account via remote access software.

And while no system is 100 percent secure, last year the UK's CESG ruled that Ubuntu scored the highest in 12 different tests of security, well in front of Windows 8 and Mac OS X. http://www.techrepublic.com/blog/linux-and-open-source/linux-the-clear-choice-for-security/

In order to have this level of insecurity on desktop Ubuntu or Mint, you'd need to install SSH, requiring an admin account, enable and set an easy password for root, requiring an admin account, if needed add/enable root user to be part of the SSH group, make sure your router and modem are perfectly configured and open the default SSH port, never turn off your computer.

Many of these steps are done though the terminal, so there is no way someone would be able to set all this up by accident.

So yes you're safe on Mint (more so than Windows/MacOSX) http://linuxmint.com/

Absolutely this. If you're going to make anything face the Internet, you need to take the time to configure it properly. There are no problems with SSH in and of itself, and as you mentioned a user has to go out of their way to make a standard desktop installation vulnerable. The odds of actually brute-forcing a good password are difficult as is, let alone if keyfiles are used properly. Windows boxes are just as if not vulnerable to any sort of attack outlined in the article, plus they've the added risk of their protocols being proprietary and thus have issues often overlooked. Don't you guys remember the RDP protocol hacks from back in the day?

And this is why the old saying, 'a little knowledge is a dangerous thing,' is never truer than with software.

You can sit your computer-illiterate grandma down in front of a Linux box and as long as it's running a window manager that looks a bit like Windows 95, she'll be fine because she's highly unlikely to figure out how to break it.

Sit your 13-year-old nephew down and he'll know that there's a root account which can change settings, and that settings are in config files, and next thing you know you're doing a clean install because fuck knows what he changed and now it crashes 45 minutes and 33 seconds after boot, but only on Thursdays.
